items.title: Custom miniature keyboard we're calling it "Hackpad"
items.text:
The image you're looking at is my very first project!

It was built on purpose to use as a dedicated Esc, Ctrl+c, Ctrl+v and Enter but I later reprogrammed it to work as a stopwatch.

The Built files are opensource at : https://github.com/mohammednurulhuda/X1-hackpad-



The PCB is designed in KiCAD.
A 3D printer was used to create the case for the Hackpad, which gives it a sleek and compact design.
This project was a great learning experience.

Honestly electronics is the thing I love!!!

items.title: Custom Adjustable Bench Power Supply
items.text:
Hey, it’s my first ever power electronics project!
I don't know if it's officially called a power electronics project or whatever, but it works! I actually started working on this about a week ago, and it's finally complete and up and running.

Before this, I had bought about 4 cheap SMPS units (around 600–1200 BDT), but none of them are alive anymore (RIP). I couldn't afford an expensive, reliable lab power supply, but when I needed a power supply for the 5th time, the trauma of those previous explosions was still fresh in my mind. That's when I decided to build my own using discrete electronics components and modules instead of buying another flimsy unit.



Here is how the whole build came together:

I picked up a transformer with a 12V-0-12V center-tap configuration rated for a maximum output of around 3A. I connected the center-tap wire and one of the outer blue wires, which gave me around 12V to 14V AC. After running it through a heavy-duty GBJ 3510 bridge rectifier and filtering it with a massive 50V 4700µF capacitor, the unregulated DC sat around 19V to 23V. To make it regulated, safe, and fully adjustable, I wired the output to an LM2596 DC-DC switching step-down buck converter module. For safety, I added a 1A fuse in series with the 220V AC input line. Finally, I connected the output to a 0.28-inch mini digital voltmeter-ammeter panel (DC 100V 10A) so I can monitor the exact voltage and current in real time.


Now I have a solid, custom bench power supply that actually lasts. I hope you find this helpful if you're looking to build your own!
